title: Florida
author: Apuleius
source: Translated by Claude from phi1212.phi003.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: ita me omni modo liberat sententia, si uinco, condicio, si uincor sententia nonne uobis uidentur haec sophistarum argumenta obuersa inuicem uice spinarum, quas uentus conuoluerit, inter se cohaerere, paribus utrimque aculeis, simili penetratione, mutuo uulnere? atque ideo merces Protagorae tam aspera, tam senticosa uersutis et auaris relinquenda est: cui scilicet multo tanta praestat illa altera merces, quam Thalen memorant suasisse.
passages.english: So in every way I am freed: by the verdict if I win, by the agreement if I lose." Do these sophists' arguments not seem to you, set against each other, to cling together like thorns that the wind has rolled into a tangle, with equal spikes on either side, the same piercing, a mutual wound? And so a fee of Protagoras' kind, so rough, so thorny, should be left to the crafty and the greedy. Far better than it, of course, is that other fee which they say Thales recommended.
passages.notes: The opening sentence completes Euathlus' speech begun in the preceding context. The transmitted text runs 'si uincor sententia nonne...'; the second 'sententia' appears to be a dittography and has been omitted. 'Mutuo uulnere' may also mean 'with wounds given in return'.

passages.original: id a se recens inuentum Thales memoratur edocuisse Mandrolytum Priennensem, qui noua et inopinata cognitione impendio delectatus optare iussit, quantam uellet mercedem sibi pro tanto documento rependi. satis, inquit, mihi fuerit mercedis, Thales sapiens, si id quod a me didicisti, cum proferre ad quospiam coeperis, non tibi adsciueris, sed eius inuenti me potius quam alium repertorem praedicaris. pulchra merces prorsum ac tali uiro digna et perpetua;
passages.english: Thales is said to have taught this discovery, recently made by him, to Mandrolytus of Priene. Mandrolytus was greatly delighted by the new and unexpected knowledge and told Thales to choose what fee he wished to be paid in return for so great a lesson. "It will be fee enough for me, wise Thales," he said, "if, when you begin to pass on to anyone what you have learned from me, you do not claim it for yourself, but proclaim me, rather than anyone else, as the discoverer of this finding." A fine fee indeed, worthy of such a man, and everlasting;
passages.notes: As transmitted, the roles appear confused: Mandrolytus is the pupil, yet the quoted speaker addresses 'Thales sapiens' and speaks of what 'you have learned from me'. The sense requires Thales to be the speaker, addressing Mandrolytus. The text is probably corrupt, perhaps originally a vocative such as 'Mandrolyte'. The Latin has been translated as it stands. 'This discovery' refers to the solar measurement described in the preceding context.

passages.original: hactenus a plerisque potatur. ego et alias creterras Athenis bibi: poeticae commotam, geometriae limpidam, musicae dulcem, dialecticae austerulam, iam uero uniuersae philosophiae inexplebilem scilicet et nectaream. canit enim Empedocles carmina, Plato dialogos, Socrates hymnos, Epicharmus modos, Xenophon historias, XenoCrates satiras: Apuleius uester haec omnia nouemque Musas pari studio colit, maiore scilicet uoluntate quam facultate, eoque propensius fortasse laudandus est, quod omnibus bonis in rebus conatus in laude, effectus in casu est, ita ut contra in maleficiis etiam cogitata scelera, non perfecta adhuc uindicantur, cruenta mente, pura manu.
passages.english: Up to this point most people drink. I drank other bowls too at Athens: the stirring bowl of poetry, the clear bowl of geometry, the sweet bowl of music, the somewhat austere bowl of dialectic, and indeed the bowl of all philosophy, which is of course insatiable and like nectar. For Empedocles sings poems, Plato dialogues, Socrates hymns, Epicharmus measures, Xenophon histories, Xenocrates satires: your Apuleius cultivates all these and the nine Muses with equal zeal, with greater will, of course, than ability, and for that reason perhaps he deserves praise all the more readily, because in all good things the attempt lies in praise, the achievement in chance; just as, conversely, in crimes even wicked deeds that are planned but not yet carried out are punished, when the mind is bloody though the hand is clean.
passages.notes: The list of writers and genres is odd (e.g. Socrates 'hymns', Xenocrates 'satires'); the text may be corrupt here, and some editors emend the names. 'Creterra' (mixing bowl, krater) is rendered 'bowl'.

passages.original: habet interdum et necessaria festinatio honestas moras, saepe uti malis interpellatam uoluntatem: quippe et illis, quibus curriculo confecta uia opus est, adeo uti praeoptent pendere equo quam carpento sedere, propter molestias sarcinarum et pondera uehiculorum et moras orbium et salebras orbitarum—adde et lapidum globos et caudicum toros et camporum riuos et collium cliuos—hisce igitur moramentis omnibus qui uolunt deuitare ac uectorem sibimet equum deligunt diutinae fortitudinis, uiuacis pernicitatis, id est et ferre ualidum et ire rapidum, qui campos collesque gradu perlabitur uno, ut ait Lucilius, tamen cum eo equo per uiam concito peruolant, si quem interea conspicantur ex principalibus uiris nobilem hominem, bene consultum, bene cognitum, quanquam oppido festinent, tamen honoris eius gratia cohibent cursum, releuant gradum, retardant equum et ilico in pedes desiliunt, fruticem, quem uerberando equo gestant, eam uirgam in laeuam manum transferunt itaque expedita dextra adeunt ac salutant et, si diutule ille quippiam percontetur, ambulant diutule et fabulantur, denique quantumuis morae in officio libenter insumunt.
passages.english: Sometimes even necessary haste has honourable delays, and often a purpose that is interrupted is the better for it. Take those who need to complete a journey at a run, so much so that they prefer to hang on a horse rather than sit in a carriage, because of the trouble of baggage, the weight of vehicles, the slowness of wheels, and the jolts of ruts—add also lumps of stone, swellings of tree-roots, streams across the plains and slopes of the hills. Those, then, who wish to avoid all these hindrances choose for themselves as a mount a horse of lasting strength and lively speed, that is, strong to carry and swift to go, one 'who glides over plains and hills in a single stride', as Lucilius says. Yet when they are flying along the road on that horse at full speed, if meanwhile they catch sight of some man of rank from among the leading men, well regarded, well known, then although they are in a great hurry, nevertheless out of respect for him they check their course, ease their pace, slow the horse, and at once leap down to their feet; the switch they carry for whipping the horse, that rod, they shift to the left hand, and so with the right hand free they approach and greet him; and if he asks them something at some length, they walk along at some length and chat, and in short they gladly spend any amount of delay on this courtesy.
passages.notes: The opening clause 'saepe uti malis interpellatam uoluntatem' is difficult and probably corrupt; rendered as 'a purpose that is interrupted is the better for it', taking 'malis' loosely, though it could mean 'as you would prefer' or be emended. The sentence that follows is an extended, loosely constructed period in the Latin and has been divided in English.
